title: Gowns, aprons, masks, eye protection and gloves: choosing and changing
audience: Cleaning and support workers who choose and change protective items for cleaning, waste, linen or body-fluid tasks in healthcare settings.
learningOutcomes: Select a gown, apron, mask, eye protection or glove type that matches the fluid or splash risk listed by the facility.
Identify which masks give little protection and which are regulated for higher-risk areas.
State when each protective item must be changed, replaced or discarded.

instruction.heading: Gowns and aprons
instruction.body: Gowns and aprons protect clothing from body fluids and splashes, and they reduce the spread of organisms by direct contact. A gown has to resist fluid, and it is put on over ordinary clothing for clinical tasks. The learner guide cites a four-level scale for gown protection, taken from a US document, ANSI/AAMI PB70. A standard disposable apron has one grade; thicker aprons are used in kitchens. An apron should fit closely around the body. Fasten it at the rear, with the tie behind the neck, and never at the front, because a soiled knot can spread contamination. Change an apron after each client and as soon as it is soiled, and put it into the nearest appropriate bin.

instruction.heading: Masks and what they protect against
instruction.body: The guide sorts masks into three groups. Cloth-type masks offer little protection and the TGA does not regulate them, so do not use them where a fluid or droplet risk is listed. Surgical masks are regulated, and levels 1 to 3 reflect increasing fluid resistance, with the higher levels used in higher-risk areas. A surgical P2 or N95 respirator is the same but also resists fluid. Fit the mask as the manufacturer directs so that it covers the mouth and nose, and tighten it on the face. Keep your hands off the outer face of the mask while it is on. Discard a mask after use, and discard it straight away if it becomes wet. A mask should never sit around the throat or in a pocket between uses, and it is changed between clients.

instruction.heading: Eye protection and face shields
instruction.body: Wear eye protection when there is a chance of blood or other body fluid splashing, and during any cleaning task where splashing is possible. Eye protection should give clear vision without fogging or distortion, sit snugly, and shield the sides and the front. Single-use eyewear goes in the bin after use, and reusable eyewear is cleaned after each use. A face shield gives wider protection across the whole face. It suits an exposure site, any chance of body fluid contact, a splash injury risk, or work with a person carrying a contagious organism. Remove eye protection by the headband or strap, never by touching the outside, which may be contaminated.

instruction.heading: Gloves: type and fit
instruction.body: Gloves stop organisms passing between skin, and they are needed whenever you handle body fluid. Single-use gloves are discarded after each use and never washed for reuse. Non-sterile gloves cover possible contact with body fluid or mucus. Sterile gloves are for procedures that require sterility, and general-purpose gloves, usually thicker rubber, are for cleaning instruments and general cleaning. Glove materials include latex, vinyl and nitrile, and nitrile resists chemicals and punctures better. Where the latex allergy risk is present, offer non-latex gloves. Keep nails short and clean so they do not tear the gloves. Use heavy-duty gloves for any task with a puncture or cutting risk. The guide also shows a numbered grade chart taken from a supplier. That chart is not adopted here, because the grades differ between facilities and the facility list governs.

procedure: Find the fluid or splash risk for the task on the facility matrix or the area schedule.
Choose the gown, apron, mask, eye protection and glove type the facility lists for that risk, and check the size and fit.
Put the items on in the order set by “PPE for cleaning tasks: choosing, putting on and taking off”.
Change the gown or apron after each client and as soon as it is soiled. Change the mask between clients and at once if it gets wet.
Dispose of single-use items in the correct bin, and clean and store reusable eye protection as the facility directs.
Check every glove and item for damage before use, and replace any damaged item straight away.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner cleans a bathroom where a client has vomited, then moves to the bedside of a second client.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What changes between the two rooms?
workedExamples.reasoning: Change the gown or apron and gloves after the bathroom. Change the mask if it is soiled or if the facility requires it for that room, and wear eye protection if splashing is possible. Do not take the contaminated items into the second room.

workedExamples.situation: A worker wears a cloth mask to clean a room where a droplet risk has been listed.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Cloth-type masks give little protection, so the worker should use the mask type the facility lists for that risk and fit it as instructed.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves in the sizes stocked, including non-latex options
Heavy-duty gloves for puncture or cutting risks and for irritant chemicals
Gowns or aprons at the level the facility lists
Masks of the type the facility lists for the risk, and a fit-test record for respirators
Eye protection or face shield for splash risk

commonErrors.error: Tying an apron at the front.
commonErrors.prevention: Fasten it at the rear, with the tie behind the neck, so the knot stays clean.

commonErrors.error: Wearing a mask around the neck between rooms.
commonErrors.prevention: Discard the mask after use, and put on a fresh one for the next client.

commonErrors.error: Choosing eye protection that fogs or sits loosely.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose snug, clear eye protection from the facility list.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Choose gowns, masks, eye protection and gloves from the facility list. Do not choose by price alone.
None has been checked against the standard text, and the US standard is not an Australian standard.
Check the fit-test requirement for P2 and N95 respirators against an Australian source before use.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner matches each task with the gown, mask, eye protection and glove type the facility lists.
Learner states the apron tie point and the mask change rule without prompts.
Learner names the item that must be replaced at once if it is damaged or wet.
documentationEvidence: Record of respirator fit-test completion for any worker who uses a P2 or N95 respirator.
Log of any protective item replaced because it was damaged or soiled.
summary: Gowns and aprons go over clothing, are fastened at the rear, and are changed after each client.
Cloth masks give little protection, and respirators need fit testing.
Gloves are single-use and must be replaced at once if damaged.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which mask type gives little protection and is not regulated?
Where should an apron be tied?
options: At the back, behind the neck
Loosely at the sides with no tie

knowledgeChecks.question: When must a mask be changed?
options: Once per shift, even when it looks clean
Between clients, or as soon as it is wet
Only when the clinical supervisor asks
Once a shift, even when still dry and intact

officialReferences.title: Understanding standards for face masks and respirators
officialReferences.covers: Covers TGA expectations for performance testing of respirators, surgical respirators and medical/surgical facemasks before they are listed on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, and the TGA post-market review of face masks. Does not state that cloth masks are unregulated, does not give surgical fluid-resistance levels, and does not confirm the P2 or N95 fit-test requirement or AS/NZS 1716: these remain UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: Therapeutic Goods Administration. Read through a summary fetch in this pass, not checked against the page text directly.
